intro: Baldenhain is a small village on the Thuringian side of the Vogtland with a dance lime local children have turned into a climbing frame. Around 1900 the inn across the road served drinks from a platform built inside its spreading limbs; the platform is gone, but the flat, chalice-shaped crown that carried it is still there. At 8.5 metres round it is one of the thickest and most complete dance limes left standing anywhere in Germany, and it is still under active care.
meta_description: The Tanzlinde of Baldenhain: one of Germany's thickest dance limes, 8.5 metres round, its flat crown once carrying an inn's drinks platform.
question_meta: The Tanzlinde of Baldenhain is one of Germany's thickest dance limes at 8.5 metres round, estimated at 400 to 600 years old.
question_answer: Baldenhain's Tanzlinde stands opposite the fire station in the middle of the village, on open ground with nothing to pay and nobody to ask. Both the regional conservation register and a dendrological survey call it one of the thickest and most complete dance limes left in Germany, measured at 8.5 metres round in April 2024 and found in vital condition. Around 1900 the inn across the road served drinks from a platform built into the tree's flat limbs; the platform is gone but the shape survives, and the village's children have taken it over as a climbing spot.
question_context: The trunk is hollow and open along one side, rising into three heavy limbs that spread out like a chalice and rest on wooden props, the classic form of a Tanzlinde, a dance lime trained over generations to be used rather than merely admired. Its age is put at 400 to 600 years, an estimate drawn from the girth rather than a ring count, the only option on a trunk with its middle missing. Somebody looks after it: the crown is held together with steel cables and textile straps and receives regular maintenance, and it has been protected as a Naturdenkmal since 1978. Baldenhain is a small village in Langenwolschendorf, in the Greiz district on the Thuringian side of the Vogtland border, reached practically only by car. It stands opposite the village fire station on ordinary open ground, with nothing built up around it for visitors beyond the tree's own trained shape and the props holding its limbs.
